tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display True when it is greater than 10, and False when it is not.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
The 10 is fixed in your program, not typed in.
tasks.starter: # Read one number and print the comparison

tests.why: 25 is greater than 10, so the comparison is True.
4 is not greater than 10. True here means the comparison was written the wrong way round.
Exactly 10 is not greater than 10. This is the test that tells > apart from >= .

tasks.fb: A comparison hands back True or False on its own, so it can be printed without an if.

teach.say: A comparison is already True or False, so it can be printed straight out, with no if at all.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Display True when they are equal, and False when they are not.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print whether they are equal

tests.why: The two numbers are the same, so == is True.
Two different numbers. True here means every pair is being called equal, which is what = instead of == does.
Two equal negative numbers are still equal.

tasks.fb: == asks a question and = stores a value, which is the easiest pair in Python to mix up.

teach.say: == asks whether two values are the same. A single = stores a value instead, and will not work here.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Display True when the first is greater than the second, and False when it is not.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print True or False

tests.why: 34 is greater than 19, so the comparison is True.
The order matters. True here means the two were compared the wrong way round.
Equal is not greater. This is the test that tells > apart from >= .

tasks.fb: A comparison is already True or False, so you can print it straight out without an if.

teach.say: > is True only when the left value is the bigger one, so two equal values are not greater.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Display True when the first is greater than or equal to the second, and False when it is not.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print the comparison

tests.why: The first is the bigger one, which >= reports as True.
Equal counts as well, and this is the test that tells >= apart from > .
The first is the smaller one, so neither half of >= is satisfied.

tasks.fb: >= is True for greater and for equal, which is exactly where it differs from > .

teach.say: >= is True when the left value is the bigger one and also when the two are the same.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two words. Display True when they are the same word, and False when they are not.
brief: The user types in two words, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read two words and print whether they match

tests.why: The same word twice, so == is True.
Two different words. True here means the words were never actually compared.
One extra letter makes a different word, so == is False.

tasks.fb: Words are compared with == just like numbers, and the match has to be exact.

teach.say: == compares words as well as numbers. Every letter has to match, so a different spelling is a different word.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display checked. Then display negative on the next line, but only when the number is below 0.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Print exactly: checked
Print exactly: negative
tasks.starter: # Read the number, print checked, add the warning if needed

tests.why: Below zero, so both lines print, and checked comes first.
Above zero. An extra negative here means the second print is not indented inside the if.
Exactly 0 is not below 0. A negative line here means <= was used where the question says below.

tasks.fb: An if on its own is allowed; you only need an else when something has to happen in the other case.

teach.say: An if runs the indented lines only when its question is True. When it is False nothing happens, and no else is needed.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display yes when it is 20 or more, and no when it is less.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Print exactly one word: yes or no
tasks.starter: # Read the number and print yes or no

tests.why: Well past the boundary, so the if runs.
20 or more includes 20 itself. no here means > was used instead of >= .
One below the boundary, so the else runs.
A 0 is a number like any other and belongs in the else.

tasks.fb: 20 or more means >= 20, and the exact boundary is always the test worth writing.

teach.say: else catches every case the if did not. Mind the boundary: 7 or more means >= 7, so 7 itself counts.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display match when the word is amber, and no match when it is not.
brief: The user types in one word.
Print exactly: match
Print exactly: no match
tasks.starter: # Read the word and print match or no match

tests.why: The word is the one being looked for, so the if runs.
A different word, so the else runs. match here means the comparison is always True.
Part of the word is not the word. match here means only the first letters were compared.

tasks.fb: Comparing a word with == needs the fixed word in quotation marks and the variable without them.

teach.say: An if can compare words with == . The word you are looking for goes in quotation marks; the variable does not.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Work out which of them is the larger and display [larger] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
When the two are equal, print that value.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print the larger one

tests.why: The larger one is the first here, so it is the if that prints.
The larger one is the second here. A program that always prints the first passes only half the tests.
Two equal values give the same answer either way, so this one must not be left out.

tasks.fb: An if does not have to print words: either branch can print a value, which is how a program picks one of two.

teach.say: Either branch of an if can print a variable instead of fixed text, which is how a program chooses between two values.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display positive when it is above 0, negative when it is below 0, and zero when it is exactly 0.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Print exactly one word: positive, negative or zero
tasks.starter: # Read the number and describe it in one word

tests.why: Above 0, so the first branch runs.
Below 0. positive here means the number was tested rather than compared with 0.
Exactly 0 is the case most often forgotten: it belongs to neither > 0 nor < 0.
A large negative value still prints one word only, so the branches must not run one after another.

tasks.fb: elif means ask this only if the question above was False, which is why just one of the three words prints.

teach.say: elif is only asked when the if above it was False, so two branches can never both run, and the else at the end catches what is left.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display small when it is 10 or less, medium when it is more than 10 but 100 or less, and large when it is more than 100.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Print exactly one word: small, medium or large
tasks.starter: # Read the number and print its band

tests.why: Inside the lowest band.
Exactly 10 belongs to the first band, because it says 10 or less.
One past 10 moves it up a band. small here means the first test is too generous.
The top of a band belongs to it. large here means < 100 was used instead of <= 100.
Anything past 100 falls through to the else.

tasks.fb: Write the bands in order from the smallest upwards, and each elif only needs the top of its own band.

teach.say: Each elif only needs the top of its own band, because everything smaller was already dealt with above it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display A when it is 70 or more, B when it is 50 or more, C when it is 30 or more, and D for anything less.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Check the rules in that order and print only the letter of the first one that matches.
tasks.starter: # Read the number and print one letter

tests.why: Past 50 but not 70, so the second rule is the first one that matches.
Past 70, so the chain stops at the very first test.
70 or more includes 70 itself. B here means > was used instead of >= .
Exactly 30 is 30 or more, so it is a C and not a D.
Below every band, so nothing matches and the else runs.

tasks.fb: An earlier branch wins even when a later one would also be True, so the order of the chain is part of the answer.

teach.say: In a chain written from the largest downwards, each test only needs its own lower edge, because anything bigger was caught above it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display 1 when the word is red, 2 when it is amber, 3 when it is green, and 0 for any other word.
brief: The user types in one word.
Print the number only, with no other text.
tasks.starter: # Read the word and print its number

tests.why: The second word in the chain, so the elif above it was asked first and was False.
The first word in the chain. A 0 here means the word was never compared.
The last of the three named words, so two tests are asked before it.
A word that matches none of the three falls through to the else.

tasks.fb: Each elif asks about a different word, and the else is what makes an unexpected word safe.

teach.say: A chain can compare a word at every step, and the else at the end catches anything that matched none of them.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Display True when both of them are above 0, and False when they are not.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print the joined comparison

tests.why: Both sides are True, which is what and requires.
One side fails, and with and that is enough. True here means or was used.
Exactly 0 is not above 0, which is where > and >= get mixed up.
Both sides fail, so there is nothing to make the and True.

tasks.fb: and needs both sides True, and each side is a comparison in its own right: a > 0 and b > 0.

teach.say: and is True only when both sides are True, and each side needs its own complete comparison.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display special when it is 3 or 7, and ordinary when it is not.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Print exactly one word: special or ordinary
tasks.starter: # Read the number and decide whether it is one of the two

tests.why: The first allowed value, so the left half of the or is True.
The second allowed value must work too. ordinary here means the or checked only one of them.
Neither value matches. special here usually means it was written n == 3 or 7, which Python always treats as True.
A 0 matches neither value, so the else runs.

tasks.fb: Both sides of an or need a full comparison, because n == 3 or 7 is True whatever n holds.

teach.say: or is True when either side is True. Each side still needs its own full comparison: n == 3 or n == 7.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display True when the word is not stop, and False when it is.
brief: The user types in one word.
tasks.starter: # Read the word and print the opposite of the comparison

tests.why: Not the word stop, so the test is True once not has flipped it.
This is the one word that gives False. True here means the not is missing.
A longer word is not the word stop, so the answer is still True.

tasks.fb: not turns a comparison into its opposite, which is often clearer than writing the test the other way round.

teach.say: not flips True into False and False into True, so it turns a test into its opposite.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number and then a word. Display open when the number is 3 or 7 and the word is not locked. Otherwise display refused.
brief: The user types in two lines: a whole number, then a word.
Put brackets round the or so that the and cannot swallow it.
Print exactly one word: open or refused
tasks.starter: # Read the number and the word, then decide

tests.why: An allowed number with a word that is not locked.
The other allowed number must work too. refused here means the or checked only one of them.
Not an allowed number. open here usually means the or was written n == 3 or 7, which is always True.
The number is allowed but the word is locked, and not turns that into a refusal.
Both halves fail, so nothing can let this one through.

tasks.fb: and is worked out before or, so an or that has to be tested as one thing needs brackets round it.

teach.say: and is worked out before or, so brackets round the or are what stop the and from swallowing half of it.
code: print((n == 3 or n == 7) and not w == "locked")

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word and then a whole number. When the word is check, display high if the number is above 50 and low if it is not. When the word is anything else, display skipped.
brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
One line of output only.
Print exactly one word: high, low or skipped
tasks.starter: # Read the word and the number, then print one word

tests.why: The outer if and the inner if are both True.
Exactly 50 is not above 50. high here means >= was used.
The inner else runs while the outer if is still True.
The outer test fails, so the number is never looked at. high here means the word is not being checked.

tasks.fb: The outer if decides whether the inner question is asked at all, which is why skipped needs no number at all.

teach.say: An if inside another if is only reached when the outer one was True, so the outer question decides whether the inner one is asked at all.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. When the first is above 0, display both if the second is above 0 as well and first only if it is not. When the first is not above 0, display second only if the second is above 0 and neither if it is not.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
One line of output only.
Print exactly one of: both, first only, second only, neither
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and say which of them are above 0

tests.why: Both numbers are above 0, so the inner if of the outer if runs.
The outer if is True and the inner one is False, which is the inner else.
The outer if is False, so the answer comes from the if inside the outer else.
Both tests fail, which is the else inside the else.
Exactly 0 is not above 0, so the first number counts as failing its test.

tasks.fb: Two questions asked one inside the other give four answers, and each one belongs in its own branch.

teach.say: Each branch of the outer if can hold an if of its own, which turns two questions into four possible answers.

tasks.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Work out which of them is the largest and display [largest] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
When two of them are equal and both the largest, print that value.
tasks.starter: # Read three numbers and print the largest

tests.why: The largest is the middle one, so both comparisons are needed to find it.
The largest is the first one, so a program that always prints the last fails here.
The largest is the last one, which only a complete set of comparisons finds.
Two equal largest values still print that value once.

tasks.fb: One comparison narrows three values down to two, and a second comparison inside it finishes the job.

teach.say: A decision inside a decision can compare values rather than print words: the first comparison narrows three down to two, and the second finishes the job.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display [number], then even on the next line when it divides exactly by 2, or odd when it does not.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Two lines of output: the number, then the word.
Print exactly one word: even or odd
tasks.starter: # Read the number, print it, then say even or odd

tests.why: 14 leaves no remainder, so the second line is even.
9 leaves a remainder of 1. even here means the remainder was never compared with 0.
0 divides exactly by 2, so it is even, and the number still prints on the first line.

tasks.fb: A remainder of 0 is what exactly divides means, so n % 2 == 0 is the whole test.

teach.say: % gives the remainder, so a remainder of 0 is what dividing exactly means.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. When the second is 0, display cannot divide. Otherwise divide the first by the second and display [answer].
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Divide with / , so the answer is a real number.
Print exactly: cannot divide
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers, check the second, then divide

tests.why: An ordinary division, so the else runs.
/ keeps the decimal part even when it divides exactly, so 4.0 and not 4.
Dividing by 0 crashes, which is what the guard is there to prevent.
A first number of 0 is fine: it is only the second one that has to be checked.

tasks.fb: Check for the impossible case first and the calculation can sit safely in the else.

teach.say: A guard is an if that deals with the one case the calculation cannot survive, which leaves the calculation safe in the else.

tasks.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Display all the same when all three are equal, two the same when exactly two of them are equal, and all different when no two are equal.
brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
One line of output only.
Print exactly one of: all the same, two the same, all different
tasks.starter: # Read three numbers and compare every pair

tests.why: The first two match, so a pair is found but not all three.
All three equal, which has to be tested first or it reports two the same.
No pair matches, so nothing is True and the else runs.
The matching pair is the first and the last, so all three pairs have to be compared.

tasks.fb: Test all three being equal first, because the first branch that is True wins and a pair matches then too.

teach.say: Three values give three pairs to compare, and joining the pairs with or asks whether any of them match.
code: print(a == b or a == c or b == c)

tasks.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Display top when all three are 9 or more, high when they add up to 24 or more, middle when they add up to 18 or more, and low for anything else.
brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
Check the rules in that order and print only the word of the first one that matches.
Print exactly one word: top, high, middle or low
tasks.starter: # Read three numbers and work out which band they are in

tests.why: Not all three reach 9, so top is out, but the total of 26 clears 24.
Every one of the three is 9 or more, so the first rule wins.
Exactly 9 counts as 9 or more. high here means > 9 was used inside the and.
A total of exactly 24 is 24 or more. middle here means > 24 was used.
A total of 23 misses high but clears 18 comfortably.
The total is exactly 18, and 18 or more includes it. low here means > 18 was used.
A total of 17 is one short, so nothing matches and the else runs.

tasks.fb: Keep the rules in the order given, because an earlier branch wins even when a later one would also be True.

teach.say: Both of these are True, so the order of the branches decides the answer: the first True branch wins and the rest are skipped.

tasks.q: With wind 15, visibility 8 and the alarm off, is each condition True or False?
tasks.fb: Work each side out on its own first, then join them with and, or or not.

info.title: One = or two
info.text: A single = stores a value and == compares two. Mixing them up is one of the first bugs every programmer meets.

info.title: No switch here
info.text: Some languages have a switch statement for choosing between many options. Python does the same job with elif.

info.title: Unreachable code
info.text: If a band that catches everything is tested first, no branch below it can ever run - those lines are unreachable.

info.title: Same as the gates
info.text: and, or and not behave exactly like the AND, OR and NOT gates you draw truth tables for in topic 2.4.

info.title: Flatten it
info.text: A nested if can often be replaced by one condition joined with and, which is easier to read and easier to test.

info.title: Read the wording
info.text: 'At least', 'no more than' and 'over' all mean different things. Write the boundary value down before you code it.
